description: U.S. Bancorp, a financial services holding company, provides various financial services to individuals, businesses, institutional organizations, governmental entities, and other financial institutions
description_full: U.S. Bancorp, a financial services holding company, provides various financial services to individuals, businesses, institutional organizations, governmental entities, and other financial institutions in the United States. The company operates through Wealth, Corporate, Commercial and Institutional Banking; Consumer and Business Banking; Payment Services; and Treasury and Corporate Support segments. It offers depository services, including checking accounts, savings accounts, and time certificate contracts; and lending services, such as traditional credit products and credit card services, lease financing and import/export trade, agricultural finance, asset-backed lending, and other products. The company also provides cash management, capital markets, and trust and investment management services; and ancillary services comprising capital markets, treasury management, and receivable lock-box collection services to corporate and governmental entity customers. In addition, it offers asset management and fiduciary services for individuals, estates, foundations, business corporations, and charitable organizations; and investment and insurance products to its customers principally within its domestic markets, as well as fund administration services to mutual and other funds. Further, the company provides corporate and purchasing card, and corporate trust services; and credit card services, merchant and ATM processing, mortgage banking, insurance, brokerage and leasing services. U.S. Bancorp was founded in 1863 and is headquartered in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

financial_summary: U.S. Bancorp is a large-cap financial services business with a $92.4B market cap on $28.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.3) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Price sits 28% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: 36 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 33% operating margin is roughly in line with the Financial Services median (29%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.25x).
It accounts for 0.7% of sector revenue and 0.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 513 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 26% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 22% and a beta of 1.03, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $409.8M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 37% in the 2022 bear market and 76% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $46.44 (margin of safety -28%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 21% above its 10-year median.
The 22 covering analysts target $68.80 on average, 16% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.32).
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 2.87% and an efficiency ratio of 55% (lean).
It earns a 12% return on equity.
hlth: CET1 capital of 12.9% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 1.45% of the book.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.8% over 3 years, 4.3% over 5 years and 3.5% over 10 years.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 86%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $9.7M sold).
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (0.5% in buybacks and 3.6% in dividends).
The share count has grown 1.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 36 consecutive years, raising it 4.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 70,000 employees, each generates about $409K of revenue, 0.8x the Financial Services median, and revenue has grown 3.5% a year across its filed history.
CEO pay is $4.7M (12x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
